name: Oyo Empire
summary: A Yoruba empire in present-day Nigeria and Benin, built on trade and cavalry. From the late 16th to the early 18th century it was one of the most powerful states in West Africa.

location.value: Western Nigeria and Benin, centred on Oyo-Ile in the savannah north of the forest.

terrain.value: Open savannah, which suited cavalry, south of the Niger river.

climate.value: Tropical savannah with a long dry season.

resources.value: Farmland, horses bought from the north, cloth and trade goods.

population.value: No reliable estimate; Oyo-Ile may have had over 100,000 people.

urbanisation.value: Oyo-Ile was a large walled city.

disease.value: Tsetse flies in the forest limited the use of horses further south.

migration.value: Yoruba refugees moved south after the empire’s collapse in the 19th century.

economicBase.value: Farming, crafts and trade, including the Atlantic slave trade through the coast.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with the north (horses) and the Atlantic coast through Porto-Novo.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; wealth came from trade and tribute.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells; tribute from subject kingdoms such as Dahomey.

inequality.value: The Alaafin, nobles and warriors above farmers and slaves.

governmentType.value: A monarchy (the Alaafin) checked by a council of nobles, the Oyo Mesi.

keyRulers.value: Oranyan (legendary founder), Abiodun (1770–1789), Bashorun Gaha (powerful chief 1754–1774).

succession.value: The Oyo Mesi could force an Alaafin to commit suicide if he lost their confidence.

institutions.value: The Oyo Mesi council and the Ogboni earth cult balanced royal power.

stability.value: Long stable; then a power struggle between chiefs in the 18th century.

eliteConflict.value: The chief minister Bashorun Gaha dominated and forced several kings to die (1754–1774).

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry was the main military strength, with horses bought from the north.

majorWars.value: Made Dahomey a tributary (from about 1730); the Fulani jihad and the Ilorin revolt.

territoryChange.value: At its height it controlled most of Yorubaland and Dahomey.

alliancesRivals.value: Held sway over Dahomey; rival of Nupe and later the Sokoto Caliphate.

scienceEducation.value: Oral history kept by court historians (arokin).

openness.value: Traded with Muslims to the north and Europeans on the coast.

communicationTransport.value: Horses for the cavalry; footpaths and markets linking towns; messengers of the Alaafin.

religion.value: Yoruba religion (orisha); Shango was linked to the Alaafin.

languageWriting.value: Yoruba; history kept in oral tradition by court historians.

artsArchitecture.value: Palace architecture and Yoruba sculpture in wood and brass.

sharedIdentity.value: The largest Yoruba-speaking state of its time.

dailyLife.value: Mud-walled compounds shared by extended families; yams, maize and palm oil.

neighbours.value: Dahomey (which paid it tribute), Nupe, Borgu and Benin.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread in the north; the orisha religion was carried to the Americas.

colonisation.value: Absorbed into the British Lagos Protectorate and later Nigeria.

riseSignals.value: Strong organisation, trade and cavalry from the late 16th century.

peakPeriod.value: The late 16th to the late 18th century, when Dahomey paid tribute.

declineSignals.value: Revolts, the Ilorin rebellion (1817) and the Fulani jihad.

outcome.value: Oyo-Ile was abandoned around 1836; a new Oyo was founded further south, later under British rule.

sources.value: Oral tradition and European accounts. Checked against Wikipedia (“Oyo Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Early dates rely on oral tradition.

knownFor.label: Oyo cavalry
knownFor.note: Horse-mounted armies that dominated the savannah.

knownFor.label: Oyo Mesi council
knownFor.note: A council of nobles that checked the king’s power.

knownFor.label: Yoruba orisha religion
knownFor.note: The religion of the orishas, later carried to the Americas.
